concepts.label: Work server
concepts.definition: The shared servers at the work place; the work either runs on one or is destined for one.

memories.text: On the work servers the user has no root access: sudo is a modified binary that runs only a handful of exact commands, essentially switching services on and off.

fields.subject: work_server
fields.object: none; sudo only runs whitelisted commands

memories.text: Never suggest commands that need root on the work servers, such as apt install, editing system files or installing system packages; propose a user-space alternative or ask the administrators.
memories.note: user case 1; overrides the generic apt directive

memories.text: Trying other sudo invocations does not help on the work servers: only the exact whitelisted commands run, so do not retry variants.

fields.situation: a sudo command is refused on a work server
fields.insight: only the exact whitelisted commands are allowed
fields.do_instead: do not retry variants; ask the administrators

memories.text: When a task needs root on a work server: stop, list exactly what is needed, and send the request to the server administrators.

fields.trigger: a task needs root rights on a work server
steps: stop and do not try workarounds
list exactly what needs root and why
send the request to the server administrators

memories.text: Home directories on the work servers have very little space.
On the work servers install software under /local/software and keep source code, databases and other data under /local, never in the home directory.
Large downloads and database files kept in the home directory exhaust its small quota; put them under /local.

fields.situation: a download, build or database fills the home directory on a work server

memories.text: Install software from source on a work server: build it in /local/software, set the install prefix there, and add its bin directory to PATH in the shell profile.

fields.trigger: install software on a work server
steps: add the bin directory to PATH in the shell profile

memories.text: Each work server runs a LAMP stack and a PostgreSQL database server.
PostgreSQL on the work servers uses database accounts, not unix accounts: connect with a database role and password, never through peer authentication or by switching to the postgres user.
Start or stop Apache, MySQL or PostgreSQL on a work server only through the permitted sudo service commands; nothing else that needs root is available.

fields.trigger: start or stop a service on a work server
steps: use the permitted sudo command for the service
do not attempt any other command that needs root

memories.text: Installing PostgreSQL extensions needs root, so the user cannot do it on the work servers; the administrators have to.
Only port 8888 is open on the work servers; a load balancer sits in front of it and cannot be configured, except that a domain can be assigned to a server.

fields.subject: work_server
fields.object: only port 8888 behind a load balancer

memories.text: To expose a service on a work server, either put it behind the installed Apache as a reverse proxy on port 8888, or stop Apache and listen directly on port 8888; no other port is reachable.
Publish a new web application on a work server: run it on a local port, add an Apache reverse proxy rule or virtual host for it, serve it through 8888, and ask for a domain to be assigned.

fields.trigger: publish a web application on a work server
steps: run the app on a local port
add an Apache reverse proxy rule or virtual host
ask for a domain to be assigned to the server

memories.text: The load balancer in front of port 8888 cannot be controlled; the only thing that can be set is the domain assigned to the server.
Do not use WebSockets in software that will run on a work server, because the load balancer does not support them; use plain HTTP requests instead.
memories.note: user case 5; applies while developing elsewhere for the server

memories.text: The load balancer in front of the work servers has no WebSocket support.
